newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopia private grouping sees coffee exports up.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia private grouping sees coffee exports up.

text.p: The Ethiopian Coffee Exporters Association forecast on Tuesday that private firms would export 60,000 tonnes of the 108,000 tonnes of coffee the country plans to export in 1996/97.

"There is no doubt in my mind that private coffee firms will export up to 60,000 tonnes of coffee during the current 1996/97 crop year (October/September)," said Abdul Razak Sherief, Board Chairman of the private Ethiopian Coffee Exporters Association.
Private firms sold 48,640 tonnes of the total 102,000 tonnes of coffee Ethiopia exported in 1995/96 while the state-owned Ethiopian Coffee Export Enterprise exported 53,183 tonnes.
Ethiopia earned $279.5 million from that export of 102,000 tonnes, the highest exported volume in its trade history.
Abdul said favourable policy measures taken by the government in helping efforts to boost private sector involvement had created "much enthusiasm among all those involved in the coffee industry".

Abdul said the fact that Prime Minister Meles Zenawi included top private businessmen from all sectors among his delegation during his recent state visit to Kuwait and Japan had created an added optimism in the private sector.
He said the coffee exporters' group which went to Kuwait and Japan with Meles was able to strike new export deals with importers in the two countries.
Abdul said that Japanese importers in particular were enthusiastic about increasing the annual import of Ethiopian coffee from a present 300,000 60-kg bags to 400,000 bags.

"This is a good beginning. We have come to learn that the scope of export for our Arabica coffee very much favoured by Japanese consumers was unlimited as long as we improve its quality," Abdul told Reuters.
Ethiopia is Africa's third largest producer of coffee after Uganda and Ivory Coast.
Coffee is Ethiopia's main export commodity and accounts for more than 60 percent of all foreign exchange revenues, according to government figures.
